text: Ghana, officially the Republic of Ghana, is a country in West Africa located along the Gulf of Guinea and the Atlantic Ocean, sharing borders with Côte d'Ivoire to the west, Burkina Faso to the north, and Togo to the east. It covers an area of 239,567 km² (92,497 sq mi) and has an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres (350 miles), situated between latitudes 4°45′N and 11°N and longitudes 1°15′E and 3°15′W. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra, making Ghana the country closest to the intersection of the Prime Meridian and the Equator (0°, 0°). The country spans diverse ecologies, including coastal savannas, tropical rainforests, and grasslands mixed with shrublands and forests, with forest extending northward 320 kilometres (200 miles) and eastward up to 270 kilometres (170 miles). Ghana is home to five terrestrial ecoregions: Eastern Guinean forests, Guinean forest–savanna mosaic, West Sudanian savanna, Central African mangroves, and Guinean mangroves. The climate is tropical, featuring a wet and dry season, and Ghana lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones—warm and dry in the east, hot and humid in the southwest, and hot and dry in the north. The White Volta River and its tributary, the Black Volta, flow south through Ghana to Lake Volta, the world’s third-largest reservoir by volume and largest by surface area, formed by the hydroelectric Akosombo Dam completed in 1965. The Volta exits Lake Volta into the Gulf of Guinea. The northernmost point is Pulmakong and the southernmost is Cape Three Points. With over 35 million inhabitants, Ghana is the thirteenth-most populous country in Africa and the second-most populous in West Africa. The capital and largest city is Accra. The earliest kingdoms to emerge in Ghana were Bonoman in the south and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north, with Bonoman existing in the area during the 11th century. From the 17th century, different Akan states emerged from the Bonoman area, primarily based on gold trading, including Bonoman (Brong-Ahafo), Adansi and Asante (Ashanti), Denkyira, Mankessim, Akyem, and Akwamu. By the 19th century, the southern part of Ghana was included in the Asante Kingdom, which developed from a loose network into a centralized kingdom with a specialized bureaucracy based in Kumasi. Prior to European contact, the Akan people developed an economy centered on gold and gold bars traded with other African states. European contact began with the Portuguese in the 15th century, who established the Portuguese Gold Coast (Costa do Ouro) and built a trading lodge at Anomansah, renamed São Jorge da Mina, with Elmina Castle commissioned in 1481 and completed in three years. By 1598, the Dutch joined the trade, establishing the Dutch Gold Coast and building forts at Fort Komenda and Kormantsi, capturing Elmina Castle in 1617 and Fort St Anthony in 1642. Other European powers, including the Swedes, Danes, and Germans, established their own Gold Coast territories, with the Germans building the Brandenburger Gold Coast or Groß Friedrichsburg. By 1874, Great Britain established control over parts of the country, assigning them the status of the British Gold Coast. Military conflicts between British colonial forces and Akan states, including the Anglo-Ashanti wars, culminated in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, after which the Ashanti lost control. In the late 19th century, cocoa cultivation expanded through the tropical forests, supported by the British administration. In 1947, the United Gold Coast Convention, led by "The Big Six," called for self-government within the shortest possible time following the 1946 legislative election. Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana from 1957 to 1966 as its first prime minister and president, formed the Convention People's Party in 1949 with the motto "self-government now" and initiated a "positive action" campaign involving non-violent protests, strikes, and non-cooperation with British authorities. Nkrumah was arrested and sentenced to one year in prison, released after being elected to Parliament in the 1951 general election, and became prime minister in 1952, implementing a policy of Africanization. On 6 March 1957, the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories, and British Togoland were unified as an independent dominion within the British Commonwealth under the Ghana Independence Act 1957, adopting the name Ghana. The current flag, consisting of red, gold, green, and a black star, dates from this unification. On 1 July 1960, following a constitutional referendum and presidential election, Nkrumah declared Ghana a republic and assumed the presidency. 6 March is celebrated as Independence Day and 1 July as Republic Day. Nkrumah led an authoritarian regime, repressing political opposition and conducting non-free and non-fair elections. In 1964, a constitutional amendment made Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life. He was the first African head of state to promote Pan-Africanism, merging teachings from Marcus Garvey, Martin Luther King Jr., and W. E. B. Du Bois, and played a key role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement and establishing the Kwame Nkrumah Ideological Institute to teach his ideologies of communism and socialism. His centenary was celebrated as a public holiday, known as Founders' Day. In 1966, a military coup codenamed "Operation Cold Chop" overthrew Nkrumah while he was in China, led by Colonel Emmanuel Kwasi Kotoka and Brigadier Akwasi Afrifa, forming the National Liberation Council chaired by Lieutenant General Joseph A. Ankrah. From 1966, Ghana was ruled by alternating military and civilian governments, often affected by economic instability, ending with Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings of the Provisional National Defence Council coming to power in 1981. In 1981, the constitution was suspended and political parties banned. Rawlings negotiated a structural adjustment plan, leading to economic recovery in the mid-1980s. A new constitution restoring multi-party politics was introduced in the 1992 presidential election, in which Rawlings was elected and again in the 1996 general election. In 1994, a tribal war in Northern Ghana between the Konkomba and other ethnic groups, including the Nanumba, Dagomba, and Gonja, resulted in between 1,000 and 2,000 deaths and 150,000 displacements. After the 2000 general election, John Kufuor of the New Patriotic Party became president on 7 January 2001 and was re-elected in 2004, marking the first peaceful transfer of power under the fourth republic. In the 2008 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo was defeated by John Atta Mills of the National Democratic Congress. Mills died of natural causes and was succeeded by Vice President John Mahama on 24 July 2012. Following the 2012 general election, Mahama became president in his own right, and Ghana was described as a "stable democracy." After the 2016 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo became president on 7 January 2017 and was re-elected in 2020. Akufo-Addo’s presidency ended in January 2025, and John Mahama succeeded him as president. To combat deforestation, on 11 June 2021, Ghana inaugurated Green Ghana Day with the goal of planting five million trees. On 6 August 2025, shortly after takeoff at Kotoka International Airport, a Harbin Z-9 crashed into a forested mountainside, killing eight people, including ministers Edward Omane Boamah and Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed. Ghana declared three days of mourning on 7 August and held a state funeral on 15 August at Black Star Square in Accra. Ghana is a multi-ethnic country with diverse linguistic and religious groups; the Akan are the largest ethnic group but constitute a plurality. Most Ghanaians are Christians (71.3%), nearly a fifth are Muslims, and a tenth practice traditional faiths or report no religion. Ghana is a unitary constitutional democracy led by a president who serves as both head of state and head of government. It ranked seventh in the 2022 Ibrahim Index of African Governance and fifth in the 2024 Fragile States Index. Since 1993, it has maintained one of the freest and most stable governments on the continent, performing well in healthcare, economic growth, and human development. Ghana has significant influence in West Africa and across Africa as a whole. It is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement and the African Union, and a member of the United Nations, South Atlantic Peace and Cooperation Zone, Economic Community of West African States, the Group of 24, and the Commonwealth of Nations. The name Ghana originates from Wagadu, a West African empire from the 3rd to 12th centuries, which Arab traders referred to as Ghana, derived from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning "ruler of gold." Rev. J. B. Anaman proposed a historical connection between the peoples of the Gold Coast and ancient Ghana in the early 20th century, drawing on D. W. Cooley’s interpretations of Arabic sources, and suggested an alternative derivation from the Wangara. Lady Flora Shaw compiled Arabic and European writings to present the kingdom as a major African power comparable to contemporary Western European states. Between 1907 and 1911, Rev. W. T. Balmer promoted the theory that the Akan peoples migrated from the medieval Empire of Ghana, a hypothesis later supported by Jack Goody, who noted it lacked linguistic and historical evidence but became influential among educated elites and nationalist intellectuals. The theory gained popularity in the 1920s in educational institutions, especially at Achimota, and was publicized by J. B. Danquah, who used Arabic and French translations to claim the Akan migrated from the Upper Niger region and associated the name Ghana with Akane or Akana, linking it to the ancient region of Akkad. Eva L. R. Meyerowitz expanded this narrative, claiming Akan origins and culture came from the Sahara and the Near East, suggesting Akan culture was Libya-Berber or connected to Mediterranean or Near Eastern cultures. By the time of independence, the name "Ghana" was widely accepted as a symbol of precolonial prestige, cultural unity, and national legitimacy. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Climate change is having significant impacts, with increasing temperatures, changing rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise expected to negatively affect infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods. Diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera are predicted to increase due to changes in water conditions.

The northernmost part of Ghana is Pulmakong, located near the Burkina Faso border, while the southernmost point is Cape Three Points. Ghana has a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons and lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones: the eastern coastal belt is warm and comparatively dry, the south-west corner is hot and humid, and the north is hot and dry. Climate change is significantly affecting Ghana, with rising temperatures, altered rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise negatively impacting infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods such as farming and fisheries. These changes threaten climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, energy, and forestry, and are expected to increase diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera due to shifting water conditions. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to a business-as-usual scenario, with a commitment to net zero by 2060. The country's geography includes low coastal plains, forested hills in the center, and savanna in the north, with Mount Afadja (885 m) in the Akwapim-Togo Range being the highest point. The Volta River system is dominant, with the White Volta and Black Volta converging in the north and flowing into Lake Volta, one of the world's largest artificial reservoirs created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965. The Volta exits into the Gulf of Guinea east of Accra, and other major rivers include the Pra, Ankobra, and Tano. Ghana is a unitary presidential constitutional democracy with a parliamentary multi-party system dominated by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) and the New Patriotic Party (NPP), having transitioned to the Fourth Republic in 1993 after civilian elections. Presidents are limited to two four-year terms; Nana Akufo-Addo won the 2016 and 2020 elections, defeating John Mahama, and his presidency ended in January 2025, after which Mahama became president. In 2012, Ghana ranked 67th least fragile globally and fifth least fragile in Africa, 64th least corrupt globally and fifth least corrupt in Africa, and seventh in Africa on the Ibrahim Index of African Governance. According to the 2023 V-Dem Democracy Index, Ghana is ranked 67th as an electoral democracy worldwide and 10th in Africa. Since independence, Ghana has adhered to nonalignment and is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement, actively participating in the United Nations and African Union. Ghana has strong ties with the United States, with three U.S. presidents—Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama—and Vice President Kamala Harris having visited officially. Notable Ghanaian figures such as Kofi Annan, Akua Kuenyehia, Jerry John Rawlings, and John Agyekum Kufuor have held international diplomatic roles. In 2010, President John Atta Mills visited China to mark the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations, and China reciprocated in 2011 with a visit by Zhou Tienong. China has become a top investor in Ghana, focusing on infrastructure, natural resources, and manufacturing, though concerns remain about sustainability, environmental impacts, and transparency. In 2013, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad met with Mahama to discuss the Non-Aligned Movement and co-chair a bilateral meeting at Flagstaff House. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are integrated into Ghana’s development agenda and budget through a decentralized planning approach involving UN agencies, traditional leaders, civil society, and academia. President Akufo-Addo noted that Ghana was the first Sub-Saharan African country to halve poverty as per Goal 1 of the Millennium Development Goals. In 1957, the Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) consisted of headquarters, support services, three infantry battalions, and a reconnaissance squadron; by 1964, it had expanded to six battalions, including a parachute unit. Today, Ghana is considered a regional power and hegemon, with Canadian Forces commander Roméo Dallaire highly praising its military personnel. Military operations are guided by the constitution, the Law on Armed Force Military Strategy, and agreements with the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre, executed under the Ministry of Defence. Despite being relatively peaceful, Ghana has experienced political violence, with an upward trend in politically motivated incidents in 2017. The Ghana Police Service and the Criminal Investigation Department are the primary law enforcement agencies, operating in 12 divisions, including specialized units such as a Militarized Rapid Deployment Force and Marine Police Unit, which handles offshore oil and gas issues. The Ghana Prisons Service and the Borstal Institute for Juveniles manage incarceration, and Ghana retains the death penalty for treason, corruption, robbery, piracy, drug trafficking, rape, and homicide. The UN's new SDGs emphasize promoting the rule of law, equal access to justice, reducing corruption, and building accountable, transparent institutions. Ghana is a key transshipment point for narcotics, primarily from South America and some African nations, with drug cartels exploiting weak border controls and porous borders. In 2013, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime stated that drug cartels from Colombia and Latin America use Africa as a route to Europe. Narcotics trafficking remains underground, and seizures declined in 2011; the Narcotics Control Board has impounded container ships at Sekondi Naval Base carrying thousands of kilograms of cocaine with a street value in billions of cedis. Drug cartels are using new methods to evade security agencies. President Mills initiated efforts to reduce the role of airports in drug trafficking. Homosexual acts are illegal in Ghana, and a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found that 96% of Ghanaians believe homosexuality should not be accepted. In rural areas, especially in northern Ghana, witchcraft accusations are common, with so-called "witch camps" housing around 1,000 people accused, and the government has announced plans to close them. Ghana possesses industrial minerals, hydrocarbons, and precious metals and is an emerging digital economy with a mixed economy. The "Ghana Vision 2020" economic plan aims for Ghana to become the first African country to become developed between 2020 and 2029 and a newly industrialized country between 2030 and 2039, excluding South Africa. Ghana has economic ties to the Chinese yuan renminbi, with the Bank of Ghana beginning to circulate renminbi as a second national trade currency in 2013. Between 2012 and 2013, 38% of rural dwellers lived in poverty compared to 11% of urban dwellers, with 94% of rural poor households engaged in agriculture. The Volta River Authority and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation are the two major electricity producers. The Akosombo Dam (1965), Bui Dam, Kpong Dam, and other hydroelectric dams provide hydropower, and the government plans to build a second nuclear power plant in Africa. The Ghana Stock Exchange is the fifth largest in continental Africa and third largest in Sub-Saharan Africa with a market capitalization of GH¢57.2 billion (CN¥180.4 billion) in 2012, and was the second best-performing exchange in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2013. Ghana produces high-quality cocoa and is the second largest global producer, supported by ICCO membership. It is classified as a middle-income country, with services accounting for 50% of GDP, manufacturing 24.1%, extractive industries 5%, and taxes 20.9%. The economy features a growing manufacturing sector and exports of digital technology products, including automobiles and ships, and benefits from diverse resource exports such as cocoa, industrial minerals, and agricultural products. The ICT sector is vital, with Rlg Communications, a state-affiliated company, producing tablets, smartphones, and consumer electronics. Urban electric cars have been manufactured in Ghana since 2014. In autumn 2021, Ghana became the first African country to issue social and green bonds, planning to borrow up to $5 billion to refinance debt for social and environmental projects and fund education and health initiatives, despite a low economic growth rate in 2020. Ghana exports hydrocarbons such as sweet crude oil and natural gas; the 100%-state-owned Ghana Oil Company is the leading filling station provider, and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation oversees exploration and production. Ghana aims to increase oil output to 2.2 million barrels (350,000 m³) per day and gas to 34 million cubic meters (1.2×10⁹ cu ft) per day. The Jubilee Oil Field, discovered in 2007, contains up to 3 billion barrels (480 million m³) of sweet crude oil. Ghana is believed to have 5 to 7 billion barrels (790 million to 1.1 billion m³) of petroleum reserves, the fifth-largest in Africa and 21st to 25th globally, and up to 1.7×10¹¹ cubic meters (6×10¹² cu ft) of natural gas reserves. The government plans to nationalize petroleum and natural gas reserves to boost revenue. In 2015, Ghana produced 88 metric tonnes of gold, and by 2019 it was the seventh largest gold producer globally, producing about 140 tonnes, surpassing South Africa to become the largest gold producer in Africa. Ghana exports silver, timber, diamonds, bauxite, and manganese, ranking 9th globally in diamond exports and reserves. The government also plans to nationalize the mining industry. In 2015 and 2016, electricity shortages—known as "dumsor"—led to persistent outages, increasing interest in renewables; by 2019, there was an electricity surplus. According to Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana was ranked 78th out of 180 countries with a score of 41, indicating perceived public sector corruption. Ghana launched a cellular mobile network.

Ghana exports gold, silver, timber, diamonds, bauxite, and manganese, and has other mineral deposits; it ranks 9th globally in diamond export and reserve size. The government has planned to nationalize the mining industry to increase government revenue. Electricity shortages in 2015 and 2016 led to "dumsor," defined as persistent, irregular and unpredictable power outages, increasing interest in renewable energy; as of 2019, there is a surplus of electricity. The judicial system addresses corruption, economic malpractice, and lack of economic transparency; according to Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana was ranked 78th out of 180 countries with a score of 41, where 0–9 indicates highly corrupt and 90–100 very clean. Ghana launched a cellular mobile network in 1992, later connecting it to the Internet and introducing ADSL broadband services. In 2025, Ghana was ranked 101st in the Global Innovation Index. The Ghana Space Science and Technology Centre (GSSTC) and Ghana Space Agency (GhsA) oversee space exploration and programs; they worked to launch a national security observational satellite into orbit in 2015. Ghana spends 1% of its GDP annually on space exploration to support science and technology research. In 2012, Ghana was elected to chair the Commission on Science and Technology for Sustainable Development in the South (Comsats) and has a joint space exploration effort with the South African National Space Agency. In 2011, tourist arrivals numbered 1,087,000, including South Americans, Asians, Europeans, and North Americans; tourist attractions include waterfalls such as Kintampo and Wli (the largest waterfall in West Africa), coastal palm-lined sandy beaches, caves, mountains, rivers, reservoirs, lakes like Lake Bosumtwi and Lake Volta (the largest human-made lake by surface area), forts and castles, World Heritage Sites, nature reserves, and national parks. Notable castles are Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle, which mark sites of bloodshed during the slave trade and preserve African heritage; UNESCO named the Castles and Forts of Ghana World Heritage Monuments, stating they shaped Ghana’s and the world’s history over four centuries as centers of the gold and slave trades and as symbols of European–African encounters and the African Diaspora. In 2010, Ghana ranked 108th out of 139 countries in the World Economic Forum’s list of favorite tourist destinations, moving two places from 2009; in 2011, Forbes ranked Ghana as the 11th most friendly country in the world, based on a 2010 traveler survey, with the highest rank among African countries included. Tourism is the fourth highest earner of foreign exchange. In 2024, Ghana ranked 55th most peaceful country globally. Surfing spots have been identified and developed along the coastline by locals and international surfers, who have brought their boards on traditional fishing vessels. According to Destination Pride, Ghana’s Pride score is 22 out of 100. As of 2024, the United Nations reports Ghana’s population is 34,581,288; as of 2018, 29% of the population is under 15, and 57.8% are aged 15–64; the 2010 census identified the largest ethnic groups as Akan (47.3%), Mole-Dagbani (18.5%), Ewe (13.9%), Ga-Dangme (7.4%), Gurma (5.7%), and Guan (3.7%); the median age is 21 years, and Ghana contributes 0.42% to the world population. There is a small population of Chinese, Malaysian, Indian, Middle Eastern, and European nationals due to recent skilled worker immigration; in 2010, the Ghana Immigration Service reported 14.6% (3.1 million) of the population as economic migrants or undocumented immigrants, mostly Nigerians, Burkinabe, Togolese, and Malians; in 1969, under the "Ghana Aliens Compliance Order" enacted by Prime Minister Kofi Abrefa Busia, over 3 million aliens and undocumented immigrants were deported in three months, representing 20% of the population at the time; in 2013, more than 4,000 undocumented miners, mostly Chinese nationals, were deported. English is the official language; eleven languages are government-sponsored, with Asante Twi being the most widely spoken. Due to its proximity to French-speaking countries, French is widely taught in schools and used in commercial and international economic exchanges; Hausa is widely spoken in the north, especially among Muslim communities. Since 2005, Ghana has been an associate member of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (84 nations); over 350,000 Ghanaian children studied French in schools, and it has become mandatory in all junior high schools, with efforts underway to make it an official language. Ghanaian Pidgin English, known as Kru English or kroo brofo, is a variety of West African Pidgin English spoken in Accra and southern towns, divided into "uneducated" and "educated" varieties, the latter used in institutions like universities. Christianity is the largest religion, with 71.3% of the population as members of various Christian denominations (2021 census); Islam is practiced by 16.8%, with 60.71% Sunni, 9.52% Shia, and 29.76% non-denominational Muslims; there is no significant link between ethnicity and religion; approximately 16% belong to the Ahmadiyya religion, and 8.7% are in other religions. There are about 150,000 Jehovah’s Witnesses. The Grand Orange Lodge of Ghana is a Protestant fraternal organization within the Orange Order; its most famous lodge, The Loyal Leopold Lodge No. 907, was founded in 1894 by Dr. A.D. MacDonald and initially served European administrators, military officers, and merchants; it later admitted local African members, a significant shift from British and Irish lodges; today, members participate in events like The Twelfth and engage in community and charitable work. In 1994, Emmanuel Aboki Essien, a Ghanaian Orangeman, was elected President of the Imperial Orange Council, becoming the first African to hold the office, a milestone that elevated African lodges’ recognition in the international Orange Order. Ghana has a universal health care system, the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), strictly for Ghanaian nationals; in 2012, over 12 million were covered; urban areas have most hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies; there are over 200 hospitals, and Ghana is a destination for medical tourism; in 2010, there were 0.1 physicians per 1,000 people and 0.9 hospital beds per 1,000 people; in 2010, 5.2% of GDP was spent on health; in 2020, Ghana achieved "maturity level 3" in the WHO’s national medicines regulatory system, the second-highest in the African region. Life expectancy in 2021 was 68.6 years for females and 63.7 for males; in 2013, infant mortality was 39 per 1,000 live births; WHO estimated life expectancy in 2016 as 62 years for men and 64 for women; the fertility rate declined from 3.99 (2000) to 3.28 (2010), with 2.78 in urban and 3.94 in rural areas; the UN reported a decline from 6.95 (1970) to 4.82 (2000) to 3.93 live births per woman in 2017. As of 2012, HIV/AIDS prevalence among adults aged 15–49 was estimated at 1.40%. The education system includes basic education (11 years, ages 4–15), divided into kindergarten (2 years), primary school (two modules of three years), and junior high (three years), ending with the Basic Education Certificate Examination; after certification, students proceed to secondary education, with options for general or vocational education; senior high school lasts three years and leads to the West African Senior School Certificate Examination, required for university enrollment. A bachelor’s degree takes four years, followed by a one- or two-year master’s and a PhD of at least three years; polytechnic programs last two or three years. Ghana has colleges of education; universities include the University of Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, and University of Cape Coast. Over 95% of children are in school; youth literacy (ages 15–24) was 81% in 2010 (82% males, 80% females); the education system attracts foreign students, especially at the university level. Ghana has a free six-year primary education beginning at age 6; the government funds basic education, including public primary and junior high schools; senior high schools were subsidized until September 2017/2018, after which education became free; at higher education, the government funds over 80% of public universities, polytechnics, and teacher training colleges. Under the Free Compulsory Universal Basic Education (FCUBE), the government supplies all basic education schools with textbooks and supplies like exercise books; senior high schools receive textbook requirements; private schools obtain materials from private suppliers. Ghanaian cuisine features soups and stews with varied seafoods, most using vegetables, meat, poultry, or fish; fish is important, with tilapia, roasted and fried whitebait, smoked fish, and crayfish common; banku (akple), a starchy food made from ground corn, and cornmeal staples kɔmi (kenkey) and banku are served with fried fish (chinam) or grilled tilapia and a spicy pepper sauce made from raw red and green chillies, onions, and tomatoes; banku and tilapia is a common restaurant combo; fufu is the most exported Ghanaian dish and a delicacy in the African diaspora; rice is a staple, with variants including waakye, plain rice and stew (kontomire or tomato gravy), fried rice, and jollof rice. Ghanaian literature has roots in a long oral tradition, was influenced by Western literature during colonial rule, and became prominent with a post-colonial nationalist movement in the mid-20th century; the current literary community includes diverse voices in film, theatre, and digital formats like blogging. Prominent authors include J. E. Casely Hayford (Ethiopia Unbound, 1911), Ayi Kwei Armah (The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born, 1968), and Nii Ayikwei Parkes (Tail of the Blue Bird, 2009). Other literary forms such as theatre and poetry have developed with notable playwrights and poets like Joe de Graft and Efua Sutherland. The Ghanaian national literature radio program Voices of Ghana (1955–1957) was one of the earliest on the African continent and helped establish the scope of Ghana’s contemporary literary tradition. Scholarship in Anglophone Africa sometimes favors literature from other regions, such as Nigeria. In the 13th century, Ghanaians developed adinkra printing; hand-printed and hand-embroidered adinkra clothes were used exclusively by royalty in devotional ceremonies; each motif has a name and meaning derived from proverbs, historical events, human attitudes, ethology, plant life, or shapes of objects; meanings fall into categories of aesthetics, ethics, human relations, and concepts; adinkra symbols serve as tattoos and convey traditional wisdom, life aspects, or environmental messages, acting as a means of transmitting complex beliefs in pre-literate societies, as noted by Anthony Appiah. Alongside adinkra cloth, various traditional fabrics are used; the most well-known is Kente cloth, a ceremonial hand-woven cloth on a horizontal treadle loom, made from strips about 4 inches wide sewn together into larger pieces; different colors and symbols carry distinct meanings; Kente is the most famous Ghanaian clothing and is used in both traditional and modern attire.

The Adinkra symbols serve a decorative function as tattoos and represent objects that convey traditional wisdom, aspects of life, or the environment through evocative messages, with many linked to proverbs. According to Anthony Appiah, they were a means in a pre-literate society for "supporting the transmission of a complex and nuanced body of practice and belief." Alongside Adinkra cloth, Ghanaians use various cloth fabrics in their traditional attire, with different ethnic groups having their own distinct cloths. The most well-known is Kente cloth, which is a significant national costume and is used to make both traditional and modern attire. Kente features distinct symbols and colors, each with specific meanings. It is a ceremonial cloth hand-woven on a horizontal treadle loom, with strips about 4 inches wide sewn together into larger pieces. Kente comes in various colors, sizes, and designs and is worn during important social and religious events. Culturally, Kente is more than just a cloth—it is a visual representation of history and a form of written language through weaving. The term "kente" originates from the Akan word kɛntɛn, meaning a basket, and the first weavers used raffia fibers to create cloths resembling baskets, known as kenten ntoma, or "basket cloth." The Ewe people in the Volta Region also weave Ewe Kente, with main weaving centers in Agortime and Agbozume, where Agbozume has a vibrant kente market attracting patrons from across West Africa and the diaspora. Contemporary Ghanaian fashion includes traditional and modern styles and fabrics, with African print fabric originating from Dutch wax textiles. In the late 19th century, Dutch ships carrying machine-made textiles that mimicked Indonesian batik stopped at West African ports; these fabrics did not succeed in Asia but thrived in West Africa, especially Ghana, where local designs, colors, and patterns were adopted to suit local tastes. Outside Africa, the fabric is known as "Ankara" and is popular among Caribbean peoples and African Americans, with celebrities like Solange Knowles and Beyoncé wearing African print attire. Designers from North America and Europe now use African prints, gaining global interest. British luxury fashion house Burberry created a collection inspired by Ghanaian styles, and Ghanaian-British designer Ozwald Boateng introduced African print suits in his 2012 collection. Music in Ghana includes talking drum ensembles, Akan Drum, goje fiddle, koloko lute, court music such as Akan Seperewa, Akan atumpan, Ga kpanlogo, and log xylophones in asonko music. Afro-jazz, described as "the reuniting of African-American jazz with its African roots," was created by Kofi Ghanaba. Highlife, a secular music genre, originated in the 19th and 20th centuries and spread throughout West Africa. In the 1990s, a hybrid genre combining highlife, Afro-reggae, dancehall, and hip hop emerged and was named hiplife. Dances are performed for various occasions, including celebrations such as Adowa, Kpanlogo, Azonto, Klama, Agbadza, Borborbor, and Bamaya. The Nana Otafrija Pallbearing Services, also known as the Dancing Pallbearers, were featured in a BBC story in 2017, and footage from the story became an Internet meme during the COVID-19 pandemic. Chapter 12 of the 1992 Ghana Constitution guarantees freedom of the press and media independence, while Chapter 2 prohibits censorship. After post-independence military governments closed private media outlets and restricted criticism of the government through media laws, press freedoms were restored in 1992. Following the 2000 election of President Kufuor, tensions between the private media and government decreased. Kufuor supported press freedom, repealed a libel law, and emphasized responsible media conduct. The media are described as "one of the most unfettered" in Africa. There are two types of traditional construction: adjacent buildings in an enclosure around a common area, found in the southern regions, and round huts with grass roofs, located in the northern regions. Postmodern and high-tech architecture are also found in the southern regions, while heritage sites such as Fort William and Fort Amsterdam—over 30 forts and castles in total—are present throughout the country. Museums are located within castles, with two situated inside forts, including the Military Museum and the National Museum, which organize temporary exhibitions. Ghana has museums offering in-depth insights into specific regions and traditions, such as the Cape Coast Castle Museum and St. George's Castle (Elmina Castle) Museum, which offer guided tours. The Museum of Science and Technology provides insight into scientific development. Association football is the top spectator sport in Ghana. Ghana has won the Africa Cup of Nations four times, the FIFA U-20 World Cup once, and has participated in five FIFA World Cups (2006, 2010, 2014, 2022, and 2026), and has won the FIFA U-17 World Cup twice. Asante Kotoko SC was crowned the African club of the 20th century by the International Federation of Football History and Statistics. Ghana competes in the Commonwealth Games, sending athletes in every edition since 1954 (except 1986), and has won 57 medals, including 15 gold, with all but one coming from athletics and boxing. The country has produced several world-champion boxers, including Azumah Nelson (three-time world champion), Nana Yaw Konadu (three-time world champion), Ike Quartey, and Joshua Clottey.
